newsitem.title: USA: Fergie eyes a day job as TV talkshow host.
newsitem.headline: Fergie eyes a day job as TV talkshow host.

text.p: Britain's outspoken Duchess of York, deeply in debt and hounded by the media at home, is trying to carve a deal to become an American TV talkshow host, according to the Wednesday edition of Hollywood trade paper Daily Variety.

The former Sarah Ferguson, divorced last May from Queen Elizabeth's second son Prince Andrew, is planning to meet with several Hollywood studios to discuss the possibility of her hosting a daily talkshow next year, the paper said.
Several syndicators, including Twentieth TV, owned by News Corp., and Disney-owned Buena Vista TV, have expressed serious interest in a talkshow with Ferguson, better know as "Fergie".
Sources say ABC is also considering the idea as a possible replacement for its struggling show Caryl & Marilyn. None of the studios nor ABC would comment, Variety said.

Aside from a talkshow, industry sources say ABC is close to signing a deal to have Ferguson host at least one primetime special executive produced by Bruce Nash described as "adventures with the duchess." More specials could follow.

Hollywood interest in Ferguson was ignited in part by her recent PrimeTime Live interview with Diane Sawyer, which drew a 14.1 rating and 24 share, up four share points from the show's season average. Each rating point represents an estimated 970,000 households, or one percent of the country's homes.

Variety reported Ferguson spokesman Howard Rubenstein as confirming the Duchess, who has been in the U.S. promoting her book "My Story", is "considering" a daytime talkshow, among other showbusiness prospects. Distributors said International Creative Management was setting up the meetings.

"She's been getting a great many offers" but has made no firm commitments, Rubenstein said. "Ever since her media tour, interest has escalated. Crowds are building at each of her book signings. Her image has changed dramatically."

No production talent is yet attached to the idea of a Fergie talkshow, and details of the format are undetermined, Variety said. Sources said no one was sure whether such a show would be shot in London or the U.S. While Ferguson is showing enough interest to meet with studios, it was unclear whether she would want to tackle the rigorous schedule of a daily talkshow, Variety said.
"Her primary concern is being close to her children," Rubenstein said. "If this interferes seriously, she will opt not to do it, but there may be ways of working it out."
If Ferguson does agree to dive into daytime, there is likely to be a feeding frenzy among hit-starved distributors, which are anxiously searching for stars to host talkshows.
The saga of the British royal family draws tremendous interest among the American public.
"Everyone will be interested in this," one studio source said. "The question is, 'Will she do it?'"
